A message to someone outside the company
The operator approves every message that leaves the company, and four steps come before you ask.
The exclusions
An exclusion exists only where the operator has stated it.
Never infer one from the shape of a message.
**A project the operator has excluded by name** goes out without approval.
Only the operator's own answer names such a project, and your stream's brief is where that answer reaches you.
With no such answer for the project in front of you, there is no exclusion.
**A pull request to a project that has already enrolled**, with its description and its comments to that project's maintainers.
The four steps still apply.
The approval ask does not.
The work does not wait for the pull request either: prepare and sign the changes locally, and send them when the work they belong to ends.
What counts as enrolled is the enrolling project's own record, and its stream's brief says where that record is.
Do not decide enrollment from a message's tone, or from a maintainer having replied to the company before.
Everything else waits for the operator: a first contact with a project that has not enrolled, a bug report, a disclosure, and a reply to a maintainer who wrote first.
Hold an extremely high bar.

Optimise every upstream report, patch or public post for a human reader and for being received well, so each one builds the company's reputation rather than a reputation for low-quality or careless submissions.
The four steps
**Research the audience.** Read the repository's contributing guide, its issue and pull-request templates, its code of conduct, and its last ten issues or pull requests.
Read how the maintainers write to each other.
Search for what has already been discussed about your subject; a question they answered last month, asked again, costs you the reader.
**Write for that audience, in their conventions.** Use their template where they have one, their terms, their level of detail.
Run `skill://asd-ste100` and `skill://plain-words` over the text.
Neither removes AI writing tells; where your session has a pass for those, run it as well.
**Follow their conventions in form as well as words.** A pull request on their repository uses their pull-request template.
An issue uses their issue template.
A thread reply matches the thread.

**A fresh reviewer reads it and cuts.** Dispatch a subagent that has not seen the drafting, give it the message and the research, and tell it to remove everything that is not needed to understand the core message.
A reviewer that only approves has not done step 4.
A subagent with no model of its own runs on yours.
Where your session can give the reviewer a different model, do: a reader of the same model as the writer is the weaker check, though no measurement here separates the two.

**Step 4 ends with a list of what it removed, and that list goes in the ask.** The list is what proves the cut happened: three lines naming what came out, or the sentence "the reviewer removed nothing", which is itself an answer.

**The text the operator approves is the text the reviewer cut, byte for byte.** Any edit after the cut, even one line of fact, sends the text back through step 1 and a new fresh review, because a sentence added after the cut reaches the operator unreviewed.
The form of the text is not in this skill.

Where the stream that owns the relationship keeps its own rules for writing to maintainers — in its project's `AGENTS.md`, in its skills, or in its brief — those rules decide how the message reads, and some of them are owned by people through that repository's code owners.
Read them before you draft, and send a change to the form there rather than into this file.
This skill covers when approval is needed and what comes before the ask.
The project's own rules cover how the text reads.
Then the ask
**Put the full message text in the ask itself.** Not a link to a document holding it, not a summary of it, not "the draft is at …".
A link makes the operator open another document, and the operator cannot judge the message from the ask.
An ask for an outside message has, in this order:
who the reader is, and one line on what they already know about this;
**the message, in full, as it would be sent**;
**what the reviewer removed in step 4**, in three lines or fewer, or "the reviewer removed nothing";
what changes if the answer is no.
Link the research, not the message.
An ask with no removal line has not had step 4, whatever it says.
One batch, not one ask at a time
An upstream bug report, patch or public post that needs the operator's approval goes into one review batch, never a per-message "can I send this" ask.

Write its entry — what it is and how serious; who receives it and what they do; the exact text or patch; its evidence; a non-author reviewer's APPROVE under your stream's reviewer-model rule; what the operator decides; its owner — into the batch, add it under the batch's Waiting list, and tell the batch owner.
Your stream's brief names the batch and its owner.
Where your stream's brief names no batch, ask the operator for one, or hold the entry until there is a batch; a missing batch is not a reason to send a per-message ask.
What this skill does not cover
Text written in a person's own name, which that person signs off.
A message to another agent or to the operator: write it plainly and send it; no approval step.
Posting a release the pipeline publishes from approved template text: the template was approved once; the release needs no new ask unless its text changes.

--- name: plain-words description: "Use before you send or publish any text a person reads: an ask, a spec, a Dispatch comment, a message to a colleague, a pull-request body, a commit message, a report, a status update.
Also use before you answer a question a person asked, and before a draft goes to a reviewer.
It removes empty verb phrases and replaces each with the literal thing."
Say the literal thing
Delete the empty verb phrases agents keep using, and say the literal thing instead.
Run this over your text before you send it.
It takes a minute and it is not optional.
Answering a question
Answer the exact question, only it, in the order it was asked, because anything else reads as evasion and the question comes again.
Start from what happens, not from a setting, a flag or a name: the reader can reach the setting from the behaviour, not the reverse.
Define each term where you first use it, in literal words.
No analogy: the reader cannot tell which part of one is true.
Before you send
A fresh session that has only what the reader has removes what the reader does not need, and lists every term it cannot define.
Fix each listed term.
A reviewer that reads only to approve has not done this step, so the two lists are what show it ran.
The check runs on the text going to the reader, never on the instructions you give that session or on what it sends back, which would never end.
The test
Take the verb phrase out and ask: **what literally happens?** Write that.
If you cannot say what happens, you did not know, and the phrase hid it from you as well as from the reader.
The phrases
| Never | What to write |
| land the change, land the PR | merge it, release it, deploy it, apply it — whichever one it is |
| unblock the work | X can start once Y merges |
| name the problem, name the owner, name a date | say the problem; who owns it is X; Y is left, and at the measured rate it ends on <date> |
| it pays for itself, that pays | it costs $16,306 and returns $60,379 a month |
| carry it to X, carry the finding | tell X; send it to X; put it on the issue |
| this shows the gap, the number shows | the gap is 12 of 30; the number is 1.17 |
You reach for "land" when you cannot say whether the thing merged, released or deployed.
If you can say which, say it.
If you cannot, that is the sentence — "it is approved and not merged" — and it is more useful than any verb.
On the "name the X" row, use the test: delete "name".
If the sentence then says what happens, keep it that way; if it says nothing, you had not decided the action, so decide it and write it.
Do not shout
No ALL-CAPS headings.
No ALL-CAPS phrases for emphasis.
Bold only where a number, a name or a choice needs to be found again.
The reason it appears: an agent writes a long passage, cannot find its point, and puts a handle on it so a reader can.
**The handle is a symptom.
Cut the passage instead.** A paragraph that needs a shouted header to be skimmable is a paragraph nobody should have to skim.
The same goes for a message to another agent.
A capitalised line in a brief reads as an instruction shouted twice, and a reader who sees three of them stops seeing any.
What stays
Plain verbs that describe a real action stay: merge, delete, send, read, measure, kill a process by pid, repoint a link.
The rule is against phrases that sound like an action and name none.
A term of art stays when it is the literal name of the thing: a merge queue merges, a garbage collector collects, a sweep sweeps.
Where this fits
`skill://asd-ste100` constrains grammar and vocabulary for a reader whose first language may not be English.
This skill removes verb phrases that carry no fact.
Neither removes AI writing tells, so where your session has a pass for those it is a third one.
Run them all on an outside message (`skill://outside-message`); run this one on everything.
The two passes themselves — the structural one and the one that removes the writing that marks text as an agent's — are `skill://plain-words/references/mechanics.md`.
One kind of text may also have a form skill of its own — a comment to another project's maintainers, a document a buyer reads — where the operator ships one; your stream's brief names it.
This skill holds for all text either way.
--- name: simplify-settled-diff description: "Simplify settled, recently changed code for clarity, reuse, quality, and efficiency while preserving behavior.
Use after implementation and before review."
argument-hint: "[blank to simplify current branch changes, or describe what to simplify]" ---
Simplify recently changed code for clarity, reuse, quality, and efficiency while preserving exact behavior.
Prioritize readable, explicit code over compact code — fewer lines is not the goal.
Legion's fork of the MIT-licensed Compound Engineering `ce-simplify-code` skill (LICENSE beside this file), renamed so a session that also installs the upstream pool loads one of the two by name.
Step 1: Identify scope
Resolve the simplification scope in this order:
**User-named scope** is authoritative; do not widen it.
**Otherwise, in git**, use the current branch versus its base.
Without a usable base, use staged and unstaged changes (`git diff HEAD`).
**Outside git or without a diff**, use files the user named or that were edited earlier in the conversation.

If none of the above produces a non-empty scope, stop and ask the user what to simplify rather than guessing, with the host's blocking question tool, matched by capability and not by another host's name.
A tool in the current list exists; never call a question tool to ask whether it exists.
Where the list names one that is not loaded, load it with the host's tool-discovery primitive.
Fall back to numbered options on the user-visible chat surface only where the host lists no such tool or a real call to it errors.
Never silently skip the question.
**Preflight.** Every file of the scope is in the pass: documentation, workflow and configuration files as much as code, and a scope that holds no code at all still runs.
A pass that drops the documentation drops the files a wrong procedure lives in, which is the failure this rule exists to stop.
Read generated, vendored and lockfile content for what it shows and edit none of it.
This is never a size gate: explicit small scopes still run, and callers own any size or cost threshold.
Report the review, apply and verification outcomes together; do not open one task per reviewer.
Step 2: Launch 3 review agents in parallel

Dispatch three generic subagents — code-reuse, code-quality, and efficiency reviewers — via the platform's subagent primitive (`Agent`/`Task` in Claude Code, `spawn_agent` in Codex) where available; otherwise run the reviews inline or serially.

For each reviewer, read its prompt asset from this skill's directory and pass the **full file content** as the subagent's prompt, together with the resolved scope (the full diff or file set) so it has complete context:
Do not paraphrase these rubrics from memory — read each file and pass it verbatim, or the reviewer loses the gating rules that keep the pass behavior-preserving.

**Bounded dispatch.** Launch only as many reviewers as the harness accepts at once, and read a concurrency or active-agent-limit error as backpressure: leave the reviewer queued and retry when a slot frees, rather than record it as a reviewer failure.
Where a dispatch fails for a reason that survives correcting the call, run that reviewer's pass inline with the same prompt asset and say so in one line.
**Agent.** In Oh My Pi, dispatch each persona as the bundled reviewer, `task(agent="reviewer")`.
Each runs as a job of its own, so `wait` for its result and read the findings from what it returns.
Which model that agent runs on is the operator's configuration.
**Permission mode.** Omit the `mode` parameter on the dispatch call so the user's configured permission settings apply.
Step 3: Fix issues
Proceed only after all three review outcomes are complete, whether returned by subagents or produced inline.
Apply worthwhile findings directly; record false positives and low-value findings as skipped without asking the user.
Inspect beyond the resolved scope when needed to evaluate a finding, but edit only that scope and its necessary import/export seams.
For a user-named file or directory scope, those seams must also be inside it; skip any fix that would edit outside the mutation boundary.
Each fix must preserve outputs, errors, side effects, and ordering.
If that cannot be established, skip it.

**A defect you see is reported, never dropped.** A problem outside what this pass may change — a wrong procedure in a document, a workflow step that cannot work, a check that cannot fail — is written into the summary with its file, its line and what is wrong, and never recorded as out of scope.
This pass applies only behaviour-preserving fixes, so the caller makes that fix outside the pass and proves it again.
The pass that stays silent is the one that let the defect reach review.

An interface or data shape that existed only in an earlier iteration of the current unshipped scope is not protected behavior once you verify it has no deployed, persisted, public, external, dependent-branch, or in-repo caller outside the resolved scope.
Remove that compatibility path only when every required caller update fits the existing mutation boundary; otherwise preserve it.
**Never simplify away a safety check.** Preserve trust-boundary validation, data-loss protection, security checks, and accessibility affordances.
Skip any finding that would thin or remove one.

**Honor a plan the caller passed as context.** A plan the brief names as context is not scope: preserve each decision it marks `session-settled:`, including a duplication or a separation it made on purpose.
Step 4: Verify behavior is preserved
Run this step only when a fix was applied.
Run the typecheck, lint or build of the packages the fixes touched, and the tests that cover the changed code, by name.
Run no whole test suite: CI runs each suite when the branch is pushed.
A pass that applied nothing left the head as it was, so there is nothing to verify: record `no fix applied; head unchanged, no verification run` in the summary and go to Step 5.
Report failures with the check name and relevant output.
Fix simplification-caused failures or revert the responsible change; never relax assertions, weaken types, or skip tests.
If no test suite, lint, or typecheck is configured, state that explicitly in the summary; do not silently skip verification.
Step 5: Summarize
Summarize what was already sound and what improved.
Report applied counts by reuse, quality, and efficiency; skipped count; defects reported but not fixed, each with its file and line; and check outcomes.
Name the agent (or model) that produced each reviewer's findings, so the reader can see which model reviewed.
If nothing changed, say so.
Do not use net lines removed as the success metric.
--- name: thermonuclear-code-quality description: Use when asked for a thermonuclear code-quality review or a deep maintainability audit of a branch or PR diff.
Also use when asked to review abstraction quality, oversized files or ad-hoc branching growth.
disable-model-invocation: true ---
Thermonuclear Code Quality
If this skill disagrees with the code, a command's output or its `--help`, follow those and say which line of this skill is wrong.
Make your own scratch with `mktemp -d` and delete only the paths you made, each by its exact path.

Never delete by a glob in a shared directory: every role of this issue writes into the same `$TMPDIR` on the issue's volume, so a sweep like `rm -rf "$TMPDIR"/tmp.*` deletes directories another role has open.
This is a maintainability review of one diff: the current branch's changes, or the range you are given.

Every remedy keeps behavior the same and removes code or concepts, or moves code where a reader finds it without reading the rest of the file, because a behavior change is work for `skill://thermonuclear-deep-review`, not a cleanup.
The table's last two rows change ordering or failure behavior: say so in the finding.
Report
The first line is the verdict, with the short sha of the head you reviewed (`git rev-parse --short=8 HEAD`, or the sha your brief names when you have no shell):
`Verdict: APPROVE at <sha>` when no finding stands.
`Verdict: CHANGES at <sha>` when one does.
Put nothing before it: a PR gate reads only the first line of a posted report.
Then one entry per finding: `path:line`, the smell, the cost it adds, and the remedy, so the author can act on it without asking.
Report few findings, each one you are sure of: a long list hides the ones that block.
Order them so the costliest is read first: step 2's structural regressions and missed code-judo moves, then rows 2-3, 7-8, 1, 9-10, then the rest.
Write each as a plain request: `this adds another special-case branch to an already busy flow. Move it into its own function.`
Steps
Read the diff and each changed file around its hunks.
Flag lines the diff adds or changes, and existing code it makes harder to follow, such as a function it lengthens or adds a branch or parameter to.
A finding on code the diff leaves alone blocks the PR for work it did not cause.
Look for the code-judo move first: a restructure onto the existing architecture that deletes whole branches, helpers, modes, conditionals or layers.
A structural fix often removes the line-level findings with it.
For a refactor, count the concepts (the types, functions, flags and modes) a reader must know before and after.
A move that keeps the count is not a simplification: say so, rather than accept a cleaner version of the same idea.
When the problem is structural, do not suggest a rename, which hides the finding that matters.
Check every hunk against the table below, because each row is a smell this review blocks on.
For file size, compare `git show <base>:<path> | wc -l` with `wc -l <path>`; `<base>` is the range start your brief names, else `git merge-base HEAD origin/<default branch>`.
Before you report a finding, quote its line at the reviewed head.
For a boundary, type or duplicate-helper claim, also read the callers (`grep` the symbol) and the existing helper you name.
A finding built on a misread costs the author a round.
Report only a cost you can name (the table's Cost column).
A preference or a micro-optimization with no such cost is not a finding.
When a structural finding exists, leave out naming and style nits, because they bury it.
Ask for a new abstraction (a type, module or policy object) only when the code shows two real callers or two ways it will change.
With one, the abstraction is the thin wrapper row 6 flags.
Smells and remedies
| Smell | Cost | Remedy |
| The PR pushes a file from under 1000 lines to over 1000 | more to scan for every change | Decompose it first into helpers, modules or local abstractions.
Accept the growth only when the PR names the caller or constraint that keeps the code in that file.
| Ad-hoc conditionals, special cases, one-off booleans, nullable modes or flags in unrelated or busy flows.
A branch for one input value in the middle of a busy function.
A branch whose name or comment says it is temporary.
| each later change reads every branch | Reframe the state model so the conditionals disappear, not only move to one place.
Make the special case part of a simpler default flow.
Else move it into its own function, or behind an abstraction step 7 allows.
| Repeated conditionals or condition chains | each new case edits every chain | A typed model or an explicit dispatcher.
| Copy-pasted logic or duplicate branches | a fix lands in one copy | Extract a helper or pure function.
Collapse into one flow.
| Hacky, brittle or "magic" behavior, such as reading a value by its string form or position.
Generic mechanisms that hide simple data-shape assumptions.
| the assumption breaks with no error | Direct code that states the assumption: a typed field, a named constant, an explicit check.
| Thin wrappers, identity abstractions, pass-through helpers | one more layer to cross | Delete the layer.
| Unnecessary optionality, `unknown`, `any`, casts, loose ad-hoc objects.
A silent fallback over an unclear invariant.
| the type hides what the value is | Explicit typed models or shared contracts, so the control flow gets simpler.
| Feature logic in shared paths.
Implementation details leaking through APIs.
Logic in the wrong file, layer or package.
| every caller of the shared path pays | Move it to the package whose existing code already reads or writes that data (`grep` its type).
| A bespoke helper where the repository already has one that does the same | two helpers drift apart | Reuse the existing helper; name it as `path:line`.
| A module that became more coupled (a new import of another package), stateful (new module-level state) or hard to scan.
Orchestration mixed with business logic.
| a change to one concern touches the others | Split into focused modules.
Separate orchestration from business logic.
| Independent work run in sequence | an order nothing needs | Run it in parallel, only when the parallel code is also simpler.
| Related updates that can leave state half-applied | a failure leaves state no code expects | A more atomic flow.
Approval bar
A structural regression, a hacky or magic abstraction, a boundary leak, or a missed obvious decomposition blocks whatever the PR says, because no evidence makes the code easier to change.

Every other finding blocks, and the verdict is CHANGES, unless the PR gives evidence that the simpler form fails: a caller it breaks, a measured cost, or a constraint outside the diff that the PR names with `path:line` or a link.
"It works" and "tests pass" are no such evidence, because this review judges structure, not behavior.
State a blocking finding as blocking, directly and without rudeness.
A "maybe" or "consider" finding reads as optional and gets skipped.
A reviewer rates, a lead decides
Rate each finding; the lead disposes of it.
Put on the must-fix list only a finding that has to be fixed before this change ships, because a list that mixes those with the rest gets filtered by nobody.
The four dispositions the lead gives a finding are act on, consider, noted and dismissed.
Write each finding so the lead can place it: the evidence, the cost, and what it depends on.
Do not review a diff you wrote.
A reviewer that grades its own work reports no finding against it, so hand the diff to a session that did not write it.
--- name: thermonuclear-deep-review description: Use when asked for a thermonuclear or deep review, or for a security and correctness audit of a branch or PR diff.
Covers bugs, breaking changes, security issues, developer-experience regressions and feature-gate leaks.
disable-model-invocation: true ---
Thermonuclear Deep Review
If this skill disagrees with the code, a command's output or its `--help`, follow those and say which line of this skill is wrong.
Make your own scratch as `skill://thermonuclear-code-quality` says, and delete only the paths you made: every role of this issue writes into one shared `$TMPDIR`.
Verdict
The first line of the report is the verdict, in exactly this form, because a PR gate reads only that line.
`<sha>` is the short sha of the head you reviewed, or the sha your brief names when you have no shell:
`Verdict: CHANGES at <sha>` when the report has a Medium or High finding.
`Verdict: APPROVE at <sha>` when it has none.
Minor findings do not block.
Priority: trace each finding end to end first.
Minor changes no behavior, hides no error and breaks no gate; any other finding is Medium, or High when the report holds its trace, because developers who get false High findings stop listening.
Scope
Audit the checked-out branch.

Report issues in code its diff adds or modifies, in the unchanged consumers check 2 finds, and in the PR body's claims (check 6), because the author fixes only this diff and the diff never shows them.
Checks
**Breakage.** Trace each change through its callers and contracts, across packages and modules, because breaks show outside the changed lines.
**Consumers.** For each behavior the diff changes, name its consumers and show that each one still works.
Behaviors: log level, status code, exception type, metric or field name, payload shape, identity or uniqueness key, timing, retry, default.
Tracing callers misses consumers, many outside the diff, the package or the repository:
alert and monitor predicates (a monitor on `status:error` stops when a line goes down to WARNING)
log-level contracts, structured-log field names, log-derived metric filters
status codes and error-type strings in request logs, webhooks and audit records
identity or uniqueness keys that a persistence layer arbitrates on
dashboards, SLOs, saved queries, downstream parsers
If you cannot find a consumer, say so, because an assumed-away consumer breaks silently.
A change that removes its own alarm is High, because it also removes the signal that would catch it.
**Developer experience.** Find changes to how developers run or build the code locally, because no test catches them.
Examples: where or how the code reads secrets, new or renamed environment variables, remapped ports or networking, a new script that must run for a feature to keep working.

Not a break: a new alternative way to run or build, or a new package-manager dependency, unless it needs a step the README or AGENTS.md does not list, such as a manual install from a website or app store.
**Feature leaks.** Trace each feature flag or internal-only check and its callers, because a leak ships a feature to users a gate excludes.
**Intended breakage.** A high-risk effect the PR body names and bounds (who it affects, how to undo it) is not a defect, because the author chose it.
Report one it does not, or one that removes a safeguard or feature gate.
**PR body claims.** Attack each safety or correctness claim in the PR body, because the diff does not show whether a claim in prose is true.
Attack these first:
Order, not coverage: after a pipeline sanitizes, can any later pass create or recreate what the sanitizer neutralized?
An input called safe because another program escapes it depends on that program: rate the finding as if it did not.
Security Guidelines
For each row whose surface the diff touches, answer with a file:line citation, because an answer without one cannot be checked.
| Tag | If the diff touches… | Answer, with file:line |
| `authz` | an authorization or refusal check, or a new route, command, or tool | who may call it, who may not, where the diff enforces that, and what the unauthorized caller gets |
| `secret` | a token, grant, secret file, credential helper, or its lifetime | what widened: who can read it, for how long, in which process |

| `untrusted-input` | a subprocess, argv, path, template, or query built from text an outside party controls (an issue body, a PR comment, a webhook payload, model output) | the boundary that neutralizes it, and whether any later pass can re-create what it neutralized (order, not coverage) |

| `prompt` | a prompt that embeds untrusted text into an agent's instructions | what delimits the untrusted region, and what the agent may do if it obeys that text (OWASP LLM01 prompt injection, LLM06 excessive agency) |
| `supply-chain` | a dependency, lockfile, base image, or GitHub Action | the version, the pin (a digest or a SHA checked against its tag), and the permissions the workflow runs with |
| `sandbox` | a sandbox or pod manifest, a capability, or a network policy | which isolation property changed, and against whom |
| `agent-def` | an agent definition, skill, role prompt, `.omp/` config, or `AGENTS.md` | whether this diff can steer its own reviewers, and, if so, what a reviewer must check by hand |

| `transport` | TLS or certificate verification, a signature, an HMAC, a randomness source, or a read or write that untrusted input sizes with no bound | what changed, the check or bound it relies on, and the ASVS identifier it maps to |
Cite an OWASP ASVS v5.0.0 identifier where one applies (`v5.0.0-1.2.5` style), so the author can find it.
A security finding with no stated exploit path is hardening, ranked Minor.
One that states an exploit path is its own finding at its real priority, so no exploit is filed as optional.
Report at most two hardening items, ranked, and put the rest in one paragraph, so they do not bury findings.
Start each security finding with its row's tag, `Security[<tag>]:`, so readers can count findings by row.

End the report with one `Security:` line, because the Legion reviewer copies it: each touched row's tag and its answer with file:line, or `Security: no sensitive surface in this diff.` when the diff touches none.
Findings
Never report a finding whose open question you can settle by reading code, because the author cannot act on a guess.
When you cannot settle it, say what you searched and where.
PR discussion
Only after your own audit, so others' findings do not steer it, and only with a Medium or High finding on a branch that has a PR:
Read the PR/MR's comments and review comments, bots' included, with `gh` or `glab`.
Check their findings in the code: a comment is not evidence.
Include the valid ones you missed; for one you share, add their evidence if yours lacks it.
Mark each finding that came from that discussion, so readers can tell it from yours.
A reviewer rates, a lead decides
Rate each finding; the lead disposes of it.
Put on the must-fix list only a finding that has to be fixed before this change ships, because a list that mixes those with the rest gets filtered by nobody.
The four dispositions the lead gives a finding are act on, consider, noted and dismissed.
Write each finding so the lead can place it: the trace, the consumer it breaks, and what it depends on.
Do not review a diff you wrote.
A reviewer that grades its own work reports no finding against it, so hand the diff to a session that did not write it.
